html:
The map's label for the Māori of New Zealand in 1530 and 1600, two to three centuries after their ancestors arrived from East Polynesia, around 1320 to 1350.

By the 1500s Māori life had moved far from that of the first settlers. The moa and other big birds were gone, so people relied more on fish, shellfish, fern root and gardens of kūmara, the sweet potato. Kūmara grew only in the warmer north and had to be stored in pits through the winter. As numbers grew, so did competition for land, and communities built many fortified hilltop villages, pā, with ditches and palisades.

People lived in iwi (tribes) and hapū (sub-tribes), led by chiefs whose rank came from descent. Greenstone (pounamu) from the South Island was traded far for tools and ornaments. Some Māori had settled the Chatham Islands to the east, where their descendants became the Moriori. No European had yet seen New Zealand; Abel Tasman arrived in 1642.
